questions.scenario: A Spring Boot payments API on Java 21 spends ~90% of each request waiting on PostgreSQL and two partner APIs. At 200 concurrent requests, latency spikes while CPU sits at 15%.
questions.question: What is the simplest change most likely to raise throughput?
options: Enable virtual threads (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true) so waiting requests no longer hold scarce platform threads
Double the CPU count
Rewrite the service with WebFlux
Switch to parallel streams
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is the size of the platform-thread pool, not CPU. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so far more requests can wait concurrently with the same code.

questions.scenario: A colleague moves an interest-calculation batch (pure arithmetic, no I/O) to virtual threads and is disappointed that it is no faster.
questions.question: Why?
options: The work is CPU-bound; virtual threads add concurrency for waiting tasks but cannot add CPU cores
BigDecimal is not supported on virtual threads
Virtual threads are slower than platform threads
Virtual threads only work in Spring
questions.explanation: Virtual threads improve throughput when tasks block. CPU-bound work is limited by the number of cores; a platform pool sized to the core count is appropriate.

questions.scenario: A team creates `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())` 'to limit load on the card switch'.
questions.question: What is the better design?
options: Set the carrier pool size to 50
Keep it; pooling virtual threads is best practice
Use newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and limit concurrent calls to the card switch with a Semaphore(50)
Use a cached thread pool
questions.explanation: Virtual threads are cheap and shouldn't be pooled. Limiting concurrency is a separate concern, expressed clearly with a semaphore around the call that needs protecting.

questions.scenario: On Java 21, a service using virtual threads stalls under load. JFR shows many jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from a legacy client that performs socket reads inside synchronized methods.
questions.question: What is happening, and what are the fixes?
options: Virtual threads cannot do network I/O
The heap is too small; increase -Xmx
JFR is causing the stall

Blocking inside synchronized pins the virtual thread to its carrier, exhausting the few carriers; replace synchronized with ReentrantLock (or upgrade the library), or move to Java 24+ where synchronized no longer pins
questions.explanation: Pinned threads keep their carrier while blocked. With roughly one carrier per core, a few pinned threads stall everything. JEP 491 removed this for synchronized in Java 24.

questions.scenario: Three parallel calls load a customer dashboard. With CompletableFuture, when the account call fails, the fraud and loyalty calls keep running for seconds and waste partner quota.
questions.question: What does structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) provide here?
options: When one subtask fails, the scope cancels its sibling subtasks, and no subtask outlives the enclosing block
Automatic retries
Faster network I/O
It runs subtasks on platform threads
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency ties subtasks' lifetimes to a lexical scope. Failure in one cancels the rest and the error propagates to the parent, which is hard to get right with unstructured futures.

questions.scenario: A developer copies a StructuredTaskScope example into a Java 21 project and it fails to compile.
questions.question: What is the most likely reason?
options: It only works in Kotlin
StructuredTaskScope does not exist
It requires Spring Boot 4
It is a preview API: it requires --enable-preview at compile and run time, and the example may use the redesigned Java 25 API (StructuredTaskScope.open()) instead of Java 21's ShutdownOnFailure
questions.explanation: Structured concurrency has been in preview since Java 21, and its API changed in Java 25. Preview features need --enable-preview and should be matched to your exact JDK version.

questions.scenario: After enabling virtual threads, someone proposes raising the HikariCP pool from 20 to 5,000 connections 'because threads are cheap now'.
questions.question: What's the right response?
options: Remove the pool entirely
Use one connection per virtual thread
Disagree: each database connection is a real, expensive server-side resource; size the pool for what the database can handle and let virtual threads wait cheaply for a connection
Agree; connections are as cheap as virtual threads
questions.explanation: Virtual threads make waiting cheap on the application side, but PostgreSQL still pays for every connection. Thousands of connections degrade the database for everyone.
